newsitem.title: EGYPT: Sudan rebel chief says fighting war of attrition.
newsitem.headline: Sudan rebel chief says fighting war of attrition.

text.p: The head of one of Sudan's opposition forces said on Thursday that rebels were fighting a war of attrition to topple the Khartoum government.
Abdelaziz Khalid Osman, commander of the Sudan Alliance Forces (SAF), said rebels were trying to draw Khartoum's forces into scattered pockets along Sudan's borders with Uganda, Eritrea and Ethiopia.
"We are interested in exhausting the enemy and I think we did well in the first stage with the liberation of Kurmuk and Qeissan," he told Reuters in an interview in Cairo.

He was referring to two towns along the Sudanese-Ethiopian border which last month fell to rebels bent on toppling the Khartoum government. They had said they were hoping to advance on the hydroelectric power station at Damazin which supplies Khartoum with up to 80 percent of its power.
"This was according to our plan. Either to proceed to Damazin and Roseires or give the enemy a chance to collect his reserves and launch a counterattack. We chose the second option.
"Most of the reserves are deep inside Sudan. We are calculating how many reserves he has and where he is. It is a military plan," Osman said.

"If you start in small pockets over time there will be areas in which it will be extended. Then the enemy is finding himself not only in the Ethiopian border, Eritrean border, and Uganda, but at the same time...in small pieces."
"When the moment comes we will march in easily. The ultimate goal is Khartoum," Osman said. "Also it is our chance to work political agitation in the liberated areas."

The SAF is a member of the Asmara-based National Democratic Alliance, a broad coalition of opposition groups which advocates armed struggle to overthrow Sudanese President Omar Hassan al-Bashir, who took power in 1989 in a military coup against a democratically elected government.
It is also one of the forces in the rebel joint military force which includes the Beja Congress and is dominated by the Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA).

Sudan has accused Ethiopia, Eritrea and Uganda of direct military involvement in the rebel offensive, launched just over a month ago from the south and east by the SPLA and the other groups. Asmara and Addis Ababa deny the charges.

The Sudanese rebel alliance scored a string of battlefield successes in eastern Sudan in its first major combined offensive earlier last month. The few advances reported by either side since then have been difficult to confirm independently.

Osman said SAF forces were scattered along Sudan's border with Eritrea and Ethiopia. He said rebel forces had penetrated 30 km (miles) deep inside southern Sudan in the Kurmuk and Qeissan area, and that the SPLA and Beja held a pocket of territory in eastern Sudan near Kassala.
